headline: Democrats took Congress. Trump says veto.
summary: Democrats won both the House and the Senate on Tuesday, taking states Trump carried by double digits. In Maine, Troy Jackson beat Susan Collins. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since 1932. Trump told Fox News voters "didn't like the candidates" and said he would accept the results. He posted a red cap stenciled "veto."

cover_question.q: Does Trump have to quit now?

cover_answer: No. He has two more years. Congress just got harder.
table_question: If you lose a vote, do you have to go along with it?

5-7.script: Yesterday grown-ups all over the country voted, and last night the counting finished. Trump's team lost a lot of seats in Congress, the big building where the country's rules get made. Now the other team has more chairs, like when the other end of the seesaw gets heavier. Trump is still president, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: Chairs and a seesaw make a count they can picture. Who was right stays off the table. At six they read your face before the words, so say it flat.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them chairs on a seesaw and a count that finished overnight. Winners and losers they know from the playground. Who deserved it is beyond them, and the script leaves it out. Expect "is Trump sad?" He said he wasn't, and that is a fair answer.

8-12.script: Congress is the gate a president's plans go through, and for two years it mostly waved Trump on. On Tuesday voters handed Democrats the House and the Senate, even in states Trump won easily. Now they hold the gate: they can vote his plans down and call hearings, and he says he will veto theirs.
8-12.why: One chain: a vote, a majority, a gate with new keepers. They can track who holds a rule now, and veto is a word worth having.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether adults apply them, so the script hands them a gate and who holds it: a vote, a majority, and what the majority gets to do. Veto is a new word and a good one, a no that beats a yes. Expect "so who's in charge now?" Both sides, which is the point, and it means slower.

13-17.script: Trump asked voters to pretend he was on the ballot, then told Fox News it was not a personal defeat: voters "didn't like the candidates." Can both be true? Second: Democrats hold both chambers now, and Trump has posted a "veto" cap. Two years of blocking, or a reason to deal?
13-17.why: Two claims from one man about one night. Let them pick first.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once and is testing whether you will argue honestly. The script hands them Trump's two claims about one election and asks them to square them before you do. Kuhn calls argument a skill practised on real cases. Expect "will anything get done now?" Less, probably. Ask whether that is bad.

5-7.a: He wasn't running. His team lost lots of seats. He's still president.

8-12.q: Does Trump have to quit now?
8-12.a: No. He has two more years. Congress just got harder.

8-12.q: Why did people vote against his side?
8-12.a: The AP says high prices, the Iran war and corruption.

13-17.a: He told Fox News he would. Watch what he does, not what he said.

13-17.q: Can Democrats do anything, or just block?
13-17.a: Bills, which he says he'll veto. Alone: hearings, investigations, even impeachment.
